newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Oil, aliens and islands tax Japan coast guards.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil, aliens and islands tax Japan coast guards.

text.p: When Japan was able to muster 60 patrol boats at short notice to head off landings on a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea, the spotlight fell on what has grown into the world's biggest coastguard.

However, it is a coastguard that has been stretched to the limit this year because of the bitter islands row with China and Taiwan, a big oil spill from a Russian tanker and a sudden influx of illegal Chinese immigrants.

With 518 vessels of all types and sizes, the Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) is the biggest coastguard in the world in terms of the number of ships. But its commanders say even this force is hard put to meet the growing tasks it faces.
Despite tackling a variety of missions, the MSA, part of the Transport Ministry -- not the navy -- is running into criticism both at home and abroad.

In January, storms prevented it from immediately sending vessels to help in the cleanup after the Russian tanker Nakhodka foundered in the Sea of Japan off Fukui prefecture and leaked hundreds of tonnes of crude oil onto the picturesque coastline.
The local governor fumed, saying he could not believe the MSA was unable to help contain the oil spill. MORE OIL SPILL EQUIPMENT NEEDED
"There is no ship in the world that can operate in a storm like that," said Ryuichi Takei, vice-commandant for operations, the MSA's highest-ranking uniformed officer.

"The immediate remedy is to fit our patrol vessels with oil-combating kits, like oil fences and solvents," Takei, a rear-admiral, told Reuters. "We could also enlarge our eight-man special strike force which deals with oil spills."
Last month, the agency deployed some 60 vessels to block a group of Hong Kong and Taiwanese activists from landing on a group of East China Sea islets claimed by Japan, Taiwan and China.

The agency briefly detained, but did not arrest, two Hong Kong activists who jumped onto an MSA patrol boat when their boat and one from the MSA collided near the islands, called Senkaku in Japanese and Diaoyu in Chinese.
The two men were soon handed back.

"The difficulty lies in the contradictory nature of our mission, to prevent injuries at all costs but at the same time to firmly repel intruders," said Takei, who personally commanded the MSA flotilla near the islands last month.
"We are aware that some of the activists have been calling our vessels warships, but we are not the military," he added. MEDIA CRITICISM OVER ILLEGALS NOT CAUGHT
In February, MSA ships arrested a record number of illegal immigrants, some 500, who had attempted to sneak into Japan from China.
But the media has chastised the MSA for not catching others.
"We are increasing our contacts with the Chinese border guard, and this is fruitful," Takei said.

On June 3, a navy P-3C Orion anti-submarine plane spotted a boat carrying about 40 would-be illegal immigrants in waters east of southern Kyushu island and it was promptly escorted by an MSA patrol boat back to China, Takei said.

Besides these roles, the MSA has been asked to stem drug and gun trafficking by fishing boats. In addition, it must patrol seas under Japan's control that were increased in the recently ratified U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Its largest patrol vessel, the 6,500-tonne Shikishima, was built in 1992 to escort a shipment of weapons-grade plutonium from France to Japan. But the global shipping almanac, Jane's Fighting Ships, has criticised Shikishima's armaments, saying two machine guns and two cannons were "barely adequate" for protecting the lethal cargo.
"We aim to meet these increasing and expanded roles by replacing our ageing fleet with more high-tech patrol vessels and aircraft," Takei said.

While Takei emphasised the need to expand his force step by step, his predecessor Masakazu Henmi, now director of a safety association for pleasure boats, said the agency has long suffered from the perception of being a secondary agency.

Its subordination to the Transport Ministry means it is forced to make ends meet without strong political support for winning appropriate growth in budget, ships and personnel. NAVY GETS LION'S SHARE OF DEFENCE BUDGET

In contrast, the navy has long been given the lion's share of Japan's huge defence budget, now the largest in the world after the United States. The navy's 1997/98 budget stands at 1.13 trillion yen ($9.7 billion), or roughly seven times the MSA's 165 billion yen ($1.42 billion) budget.
"The cost of one of their (the navy's) Aegis cruisers is equal to our entire annual budget," lamented one MSA official.
"Because the MSA is under the ministry and because the government lacks an overall maritime security strategy, it has suffered from patchwork treatment," Henmi told Reuters.
